Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks. Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty. In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. A pre-prepared or memorised composition will earn you little or no marks.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**QUESTION 2: TEXT RECONSTRUCTION (15 marks)**

*Read the following text carefully, identify and correct the mistakes in it. Then copy the corrected text in your answer booklet, underlining all the identified corrected mistakes.*

It seem fashionable in some quater today to decry examinations and the ability to pass it. How far do you think it is valuable to have the skill to succeed in this formal test.
I supposed that it shows a certain capacity to coping with new problems and it probably shows the ability to express taught and ideas in a way that can easily be understood by others.
Yes, but it could equally well be argued that examinations tests only a certain kind of skill and all that a candidate needs is a good memory and a special facility, which do not depend at all on any capacity to think or to write on an original way.
Surely alot of employees rely very much on examination results when it comes to deciding whether to employ one school-leaver rather than another.
You are absolutely rite. They quite wrongly accept the result as a standard by which a person real worth can be judge. It seems ineviteable that for as long as examinations exists those who can pass it will have an unfair advantage over those who can.
Weather that is so or not, the mental effort of preparing for an examination is excellent in themselves, because even the dulest member of a class will exert themself without any ill-effects. At the same time it stops some teachers with fancifull ideas about what the young ought to be learning from putting too much emphasise in useless schemes of work. It can easily be shown that boys and girls from schools who don't take examinations had some startling gaps in their knowledge of basic subjects.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Corrected text** (every correction should be underlined in the candidate's copy)

It seems fashionable in some quarters today to decry examinations and the ability to pass them. How far do you think it is valuable to have the skill to succeed in this formal test?
I suppose that it shows a certain capacity to cope with new problems and it probably shows the ability to express thoughts and ideas in a way that can easily be understood by others.
Yes, but it could equally well be argued that examinations test only a certain kind of skill and all that a candidate needs is a good memory and a special facility, which do not depend at all on any capacity to think or to write in an original way.
Surely a lot of employers rely very much on examination results when it comes to deciding whether to employ one school-leaver rather than another.
You are absolutely right. They quite wrongly accept the result as a standard by which a person's real worth can be judged. It seems inevitable that for as long as examinations exist those who can pass them will have an unfair advantage over those who cannot.
Whether that is so or not, the mental effort of preparing for an examination is excellent in itself, because even the dullest member of a class will exert himself or herself without any ill-effects. At the same time it stops some teachers with fanciful ideas about what the young ought to be learning from putting too much emphasis on useless schemes of work. It can easily be shown that boys and girls from schools which don't take examinations have some startling gaps in their knowledge of basic subjects.

**Table of corrections (26 in all)**

| No. | Original | Correction | Rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | It seem | It seems | subject-verb agreement (singular subject "it") |
| 2 | quater | quarters | spelling; "in some quarters" is the fixed phrase |
| 3 | to pass it | to pass them | pronoun agreement ("examinations" is plural) |
| 4 | this formal test. | this formal test? | a direct question ends with a question mark (probable) |
| 5 | I supposed | I suppose | tense (present habitual opinion) |
| 6 | capacity to coping | capacity to cope | "capacity to" + base verb (or "capacity for coping") |
| 7 | express taught and ideas | express thoughts and ideas | wrong word ("taught" is a verb form); "thoughts" |
| 8 | examinations tests | examinations test | subject-verb agreement (plural subject) |
| 9 | on an original way | in an original way | preposition ("in a ... way") |
| 10 | alot | a lot | spelling (two words) |
| 11 | employees | employers | wrong word: it is the employers who choose whom to employ |
| 12 | rite | right | spelling and homophone |
| 13 | a person real worth | a person's real worth | possessive 's |
| 14 | can be judge | can be judged | passive voice: past participle |
| 15 | ineviteable | inevitable | spelling |
| 16 | examinations exists | examinations exist | subject-verb agreement (plural subject) |
| 17 | pass it will | pass them will | pronoun agreement ("examinations") |
| 18 | those who can. | those who cannot. | logic: the advantage is over those who cannot pass |
| 19 | Weather that | Whether that | homophone: "whether" introduces the alternative |
| 20 | excellent in themselves | excellent in itself | agreement with the singular "effort" |
| 21 | dulest | dullest | spelling (double l) |
| 22 | exert themself | exert himself or herself | "themself" is not standard; reflexive agreeing with "member" |
| 23 | fancifull | fanciful | spelling |
| 24 | emphasise in | emphasis on | word class (noun) and preposition ("emphasis on") |
| 25 | schools who | schools which | relative pronoun for things |
| 26 | had some startling gaps | have some startling gaps | tense: general truth in the present ("it can easily be shown") |

**Notes**

- "which do not depend" can stay: its antecedent is the pair "a good memory and a special facility". "don't" may be kept (a contraction is not a mistake in this text).
- Several corrections may be accepted in different forms: "capacity for coping" for "capacity to cope"; "exert themselves" or "exert himself or herself"; "had" may be left if the candidate changes the whole sentence to the past consistently, but "have" is the natural reading.
- Number 4 (question mark) is a punctuation correction that the Board may or may not have planned: the question is direct, so the mark belongs there.

**Marking guide**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Identifying and correcting mistakes | most of the 15 | Each mistake that is corrected accurately and underlined earns credit; a wrong "correction" of a sentence that was right loses credit |
| Accurate copying | remaining marks | The whole text is copied, with the original wording kept apart from the corrections, and with correct spelling and punctuation |

(The paper does not print how the 15 marks are shared.)

**Common mistakes**

1. Correcting only the spelling mistakes ("quater", "alot", "rite", "dulest") and missing the grammar and sense errors ("employees", "those who can", "taught", "had").
2. Rewriting sentences instead of correcting the faulty words, or not underlining the corrections.
